invented: Glycolysis occurs in the cytoplasm/cytosol.
Glycolysis uses one six-carbon glucose, 2 startup ATP, 2 NAD+, and 2 ADP plus phosphate; it produces two three-carbon pyruvates, net 2 ATP (4 made and 2 used), 2 NADH, and water/H+.
Glycolysis requires no oxygen and produces ATP through substrate-level phosphorylation.
The Krebs cycle is also called the citric acid or TCA cycle, occurs in the mitochondrial matrix in eukaryotes, and runs twice per glucose.
The link reaction produces 2 acetyl-CoA, 2 CO2, and 2 NADH per glucose.
The Krebs cycle takes in acetyl-CoA, NAD+, FAD, ADP or GDP, phosphate, and water; per glucose it produces 4 CO2, 6 NADH, 2 FADH2, and 2 ATP or GTP, with CoA recycled.
Most exhaled CO2 comes from the Krebs cycle and link reaction; Krebs ATP/GTP is produced through substrate-level phosphorylation.
The electron transport chain occurs in the inner mitochondrial membrane/cristae; protons are pumped into the intermembrane space and return to the matrix through ATP synthase.

Oxidative phosphorylation uses NADH, FADH2, oxygen, ADP, and phosphate, producing water, regenerated NAD+ and FAD, and ATP; oxygen is the final electron acceptor and its absence stalls the aerobic pathway.
A proton gradient drives ATP synthase through chemiosmosis.
Oxidative phosphorylation yields approximately 26–28 ATP per glucose, for a total of approximately 30–32; some older textbooks give 36–38, and totals depend on shuttle systems.
ATP conversion factors of 2.5 per NADH and 1.5 per FADH2 are contrasted with older factors of 3 and 2.
